p:
Yeah. So as part of the November plan that was released under the Adams Administration, there was a transfer of the B-HEARD funding that was associated with the dedicated units. So, it was about 4 million dollars annually that was part of the transfer to H and H. There had been an announcement about the program itself transferring to H and H. And so that funding had been moved.

COUNCIL MEMBER CABÁN: Has that happened?

So, the program continues to operate as status quo. The Fire Department is still operating it, and we anticipate that the funding will be moved back in a future financial plan. The other part of funding associated with B-HEARD is there is a differential that folks in EMS receive once they've completed the appropriate mental health response training, and that funding was never moved so that continues to be in our budget. COUNCIL MEMBER CABÁN: So, is it your understanding, I know obviously that the previous Mayor, you know, made the decision to move B-HEARD from FDNY to H and H. Based on what you're saying, if the funding is going to come back to you guys, do you anticipate it staying under FDNY for the foreseeable future? And also how does this relate to, if you can speak on it at all, to, you know, a developing department of community safety?

Yes. This program, as you know, is a pilot that started in 2021. It was between the Fire Department and H and H, where the Fire Department and H and H got together

and sent a unit that was responding to mental illness crisis assignments, low acuity, nonviolent assignments, together so that law enforcement would not have to go there, and that the patient would get the help they need from the social worker and from the EMTs, and we've been running this program as a pilot in partnership with H and H since then. We've not stopped running this program. We've continued to run this program in conjunction with our partners. And this Administration, I can say, is very interested in providing different opportunities for those with mental illness to get the help that they need, the appropriate help that they need. And this program is important to that mission. The fact that the funding is being transferred back to FDNY at some point indicates that it will likely stay with FDNY, but it is still being negotiated and discussed at this point. So, up until something changes, we're going to continue to run it. COUNCIL MEMBER CABÁN: And I know I have limited time, so that's why I'm just cutting in here. And I'm happy to hear that also because the EMS union obviously made it known that they would prefer it stay under FDNY. And also, we know that in

terms of federal reimbursement and eligibility, where it lives determines sort of like what funds are available to the program. Another question I have too is that, I mean, if it's being moved back, is it, you know, we had heard information about EMTs being taken off of the B-HEARD calls and not being part of that core team. What's the status of that?

So, it has never moved so it's not moving back. We've maintained it the entire time. So, if the program continues to expand, we will restaff it with the appropriate staff. COUNCIL MEMBER CABÁN: Great. Thank you. The last thing I'll say on this, and I'll hand it back to the Chair, is like, I just, I'm obsessed with this model. I have gone to several cities to visit their alternative responders and so just would love to continue to be a partner on strengthening it and talking about what (TIMER CHIME) resources are needed to also strengthen the outcomes. I know this has been said by the Chair and others, but EMTs need to be paid a whole lot more. Y'all are training folks and then losing them to all of these

other first responder, you know, cohorts. So, I just thank you again for your work, and I'm looking forward to staying in touch. And thank you, Chair.
Thank you for your support.

So, I'd like to talk about unit availability data. What is the percentage of ambulances, engines, and trucks available at any given time by borough? And for fire operations, why is it that they determine response time to be when the fire truck arrives on the scene and not when the water is on the fire?

On the fire side, the water on the fire would be a different time, obviously, than when we arrive on the scene. We have historically counted our response time for when we pull up in front of the building. To be able to accurately determine and capture when we have water on the fire would be significantly more difficult because the firefighters operating don't have contact with the dispatcher. That would have to be relayed. It would be another step. We acknowledge that it's generally several minutes from the time they arrive on the scene to have water on the fire. And

obviously, the further vertically from the ground, the longer time that would take as well.
Okay. And then the first part of my question was what percentage of ambulances, engines, and trucks are available at any given time by borough?

I'll talk about EMS and then Chief Esposito can talk about fire. It's not really easy to give you a number because it really depends on the actual day. There are some days that availability is extremely low. There are some days that we're holding assignments for quite some time waiting for ambulances so it really does depend on the volume of the day.
Okay.

And then on the fire availability, generally, we are available at least 50 percent of the time and generally higher. If we have below 50 percent availability in any borough, we would be relocating companies to ensure coverage.

Okay. Because I passed intro 1229, which is now Local Law 30 in 2026, and it requires the Fire Department to report monthly on the average number of emergency medical service

vehicles available each day and to respond to the emergency so hopefully we'll have a better counting on that. And just my final question before we go to Council Member Maloney is how is the production of the new EMS CAD system proceeding?

We're moving forward and we're all very, very excited about it. The system we have right now is 35 years old so we're excited about moving forward with new refresh in technology. We've had a contract awarded, and they're beginning the collection of information that it's going to take to get this thing done so we expect to have a new EMS CAD in place in about two years.
Thank you. Council Member Maloney.

Thank you so much, Chair, and thank you for being here, Commissioner, and for the really thoughtful and helpful testimony earlier. I wanted to come back to the ambulance response times questions that Council Member Schulman brought up. Thank you for outlining clearly some of

the causes and the ideas and solutions that you've proposed. One question I had, a follow-up, was that fire engines supplement EMS response times and is increasingly putting pressure on engine companies. So, just wondering how frequently are engine companies being dispatched to EMS calls due to ambulance shortages?

Well, going on about 30 years, fire engine companies, the CFR, certified first responder companies, have been responding to the most serious life-threatening incident segment one, two, and three calls, and that is not necessarily because there may be a shortage or a delay in an ambulance. The ambulance and the fire company are dispatched simultaneously. And about half the time, the ambulance arrives on the scene first, and about half the time, the engine company arrives on the scene first, and those engines would perform the patient assessment and provide life-saving care until the ambulance responds.

I'm sorry. I'm Paul Miano, Chief of EMS. I know we're focusing a lot on response time and the amount of time it actually takes to get

to the patient, and that is just one metric, but it doesn't tell the whole picture and the story of what my members do. So far this year, since January 1st, we have resuscitated over 200 people who were in cardiac arrest and delivered over 25 babies into this world. Last year, we provided over 2,000 times life-saving epinephrine to people who were in anaphylactic shock. Countless amount of times, we've provided albuterol to patients who couldn't breathe and were having severe asthma attacks. So, while I understand that we put a lot of emphasis on the amount of time it takes to get there, what I really want everybody to focus on is the medicine that we provide when we get there and the ability of my members to stop people from dying. And the men and women of EMS, while response time is a really, really, really important metric, the men and women of EMS, the job that they do, that's the most important metric that we should look at.
Thank you for that. And again, thank you for all the hard work of the men and women of

One of the things, I know the Bronx has a bit of an outsized

increase in ambulance delays and there was a pilot program looking at increasing engine company staffing to address the demand. And just curious, are you planning to implement that program? Any updates on how you'll measure success of that pilot program?
So, we are aware of the proposal and we are currently reviewing the staffing proposal.

Thank you. Shifting gears, I wanted to talk about firehouse conditions. In your testimony, Commissioner, you talked about how the Department is committed to the best equipment and the best infrastructure. And some of the firefighters in my community have raised concerns around structural conditions in the firehouses, roofs, and mold. How many firehouses currently have outstanding structural maintenance issues like that that you're aware of? And what are the timelines for addressing some of those challenges?

Well, if there are structural issues, we assess them immediately to make sure there's no health or safety risks associated with them. If there are, we get

scaffolding up or whatever needs to be done and then we work on allocating proper funding to ensure that nothing major occurs.
And since this is a budget hearing, does the FDNY currently have sufficient capital funding to maintain firehouse facilities in a safe condition for firefighters?

So, while we would always welcome additional funding, we do have a significant amount of funding for firehouse renovations and reconstructions. So, the capital plan more broadly includes 970 million DOLLARS going from FY26 to FY35. It's about 52 percent of our capital budget. That includes 141 million that's tied to kind of wholesale new facilities, includes things like Engine 287, Engine 268, EMS stations such as EMS 17 and EMS 7. Also includes 310 million dollars for very large rehab programs. 84 million dollars that's assigned for like smaller or single component repairs at firehouses and EMS stations. And about 434 million in lump sum funding which gets broken out into specific projects as that prioritization process occurs.
Thank you. I'm going to yield back to the Chair.

All good? Okay. I just want to piggyback on Council Member Cabán, what she was talking about. You mentioned previously in the November plan that B-HEARD program was shifted from FDNY to H and H and the funding being moved out of the Fire Department. Then you stated that FDNY has continued running B-HEARD with the assumption that the program funding will return to FDNY. What funding streams has FDNY been running this program with? And the preliminary budget included 72 million in PS adjustments. Does any of the new funding include an increased overtime budget for the B-HEARD program?

So, none of the PS adjustment in this plan was tied to B-HEARD. We anticipate that the B-HEARD adjustment will be part of a future plan, likely the executive budget. But we continue to operate B-HEARD using City funds.

I have to say I'm really disappointed in the answers. I'm disappointed in the non-answers. I'm disappointed in the

non-definite absolute answers considering this should have been much more preparation. We'll stay on EMS. Can you provide data for assaults to our EMS members, our uniformed members of the EMS?

Yes. I have that information here. In 2025, as of 10/15, that's October, there were a total of 161 physical assaults by patients and 23 assaults by civilians. There were seven patient verbal assaults and 11 verbal assaults from civilians. Aggressive behavior, there were six from patients, that's not assault, that's behavior-wise, and there were six from civilians. And we have a total there of 161 assaults from patients.

Council Member Feliz had asked that question. Okay. So, now let's go on to maintenance. So, we spoke about the Council Member aptly brought up the condition of the firehouses, and there was quite a bit of capital money that you mentioned that we have for fixing that so I'm going to go to the apparatus. What is the current total number of fire apparatus in the fleet?
So, for fire apparatus, we have roughly about 500 fire apparatus.
500, okay. And what is the average age of the fire engines and what percentage are beyond the 11-year, 364-day replacement standard?
So, the average age of our fire apparatus for pumpers and ladders are about six years.
And what are the average age of ladder trucks and what percentage are beyond the 10-year, 364-day replacement standard?
So, ladder trucks is also a six-year, and there's probably roughly about 43 that are beyond replacement.
And what percentage of fire apparatus are out of service on any given day due to maintenance or repairs?
On average, it's about 20 percent, but we have spare apparatus so there's never a company that does not have apparatus.

Okay. What is the annual maintenance cost per fire engine and per

ladder truck? And what percentage of the fleet maintenance budget does this represent?
So, the annual maintenance cost for a fire apparatus engine or ladder is roughly about 80,000 dollars.

So, the apparatus downtime that we're hearing, is that due to mechanics? Is that directly impacted because the FDNY's ability to respond to emergencies is because historically the mechanics portion of the FDNY has had its fleet workforce at inadequate staffing levels? Or are they at adequate staffing levels now?
We could always use more. I would never say we cannot use more.
I'm sorry?
I would say we could always use more.
You could say we could always use more.
And we have 167 fleet auto mechanics, and that staffing level has remained effectively flat --
How many openings do you have?
-- over the last several years.
How many lines do you have that are not filled?
So, we're actually above budget for our civilian headcount so we don't technically have any vacancies.
Okay. On your spare apparatuses, what is the average age?
I'll have to get back to you with that number.

All right. Now we're going to switch if everybody can take a look at the board, the screen. So, we spoke earlier about the capital money, and I wanted Council Member Maloney, especially because she asked the question, because it doesn't track with what we're seeing. So, the following photos show water damage at Engine Company 59, Ladder 30 in Manhattan. These pictures show water damage that has corroded the ceilings, the walls of the firehouse. There is a pipe that is clearly showing that water has been leaking out of. The water

has damaged the steps inside the firehouse from the constant leak, and we see steps with stain and buildup. Would you consider these safe or healthy conditions for members to work in?

Well, the safety and health of our members is always the utmost importance. When we see water infiltration, we immediately dispatch staff to survey to see if it's something they could patch or if it's something that needs a total roof repair. For something like this, this location needs to be repointed, which is a larger capital program. So, we will do what we can to ensure that there is minor infiltration until we can get to the larger roof repair.

So, what is the 970 million that you have appropriated to, if not cleaning these up? We can answer that later. Next, we have the roof leak at Engine 262 in Astoria, Queens, that has at least five work orders reported on 1/25 of '23, 4/29 of '23, 11/25 of '25, 1/7 of '26, 2/15 of '26. In the photo, you will see a drop ceiling that is missing tiles from what looks like a leak. The tiles are filled with heavy water stains. There is another picture of the ceiling

covered where tiles seem to be missing. There is a picture of a blue wall surrounding a window air conditioning unit with what appears to be the outlet of the unit to the left of the unit. What is the timeline for repairs of this nature?
So, this location, we actually are in the process of doing a lot of the sampling around the and we are working on submitting this work.

How much are safety conditions like water dripping into air conditioning units and outlets taken into consideration? This was first reported over three years ago. When did facilities start to do the work that you're referring to?
I'd have to go back and check my notes to see when this was first reported.
I told you it was first reported on 1/25 of '23.
Well, I have to double check with my staff on when they received the request.
Do you have the information of when you began the work? You said it's currently being worked on.
Yes. So, they've did some of these testings in the past two weeks.

In the last two weeks. Okay. Next we have pictures of the first floor at Engine Four Ladder 15. The first picture shows the crumbled support wall of the firehouse between the two apparatus doors. Next, we have a picture of the rear wall of the apparatus floor, which we also see crumbling. There are so many areas with ceiling missing tiles around light fixtures, with either water-stained tiles surrounding the missing tiles, so we can assume the tiles are missing due to water damage from the leak. How dangerous would you say the crumbling support wall between the two apparatus doors is to the integrity of the building?
So, there were no work orders called in for this.
I can't hear you.
There was no work orders called in for this work, so if there is, I would like them to be forwarded.

Yeah. We're going to forward you those work orders. We do have them. This is the roof of Engine 229 Ladder 146 in Brooklyn. The photo shows ceiling damage and the roof has sunk from its proper place. The roof should be in line with the metal rail on the exterior wall. The picture shows the roof about one foot below the metal rail. The next picture shows the water damage happening inside the firehouse above the cooling heating unit. Work orders for this were submitted on 10-5-21 for the section of the ceiling collapse on the third floor; 10-22-25 of the roof line sagging, water pooling on the roof and leaking to the third floor; 1-29-26, no heat; 2-11-26, the Nederman system out of service, and the Nederman system is the vacuum, for those who don't know, that the Fire Department attaches to their apparatus exhaust system to capture noxious exhaust and diesel fumes; 2-18-26, Nederman system still out of service; 2-26-26, no heat, Nederman system still out of service.

So, I'm going to ask you four questions and then Council Member Maloney has a follow-up. What was the delay in repair of this roof cave-in? What is the function of the Nederman system beyond what I described? And how does having it out of service for over a month affect the firehouse and its members?

So, in regards to the roof, I will have to do look into more information about this specific roof issue here. In regards to the Nederman, the Nederman system, like you said, it attaches to the exhaust of all the apparatus and pulls all the fumes from the apparatus outside the building. We have staff on call that repairs the Nederman. For this specific issue, I would have to find out what it was. Were they waiting on a part? Not sure what it is, but I will find out about that. But when a Nederman issue occurs, we have in-house staff that immediately responds to correct the issue.
Just one moment. We're out of respect for time for my Colleague, Pierina Sanchez. She has a couple of questions, and then we can get back to the slideshow.

Amazing. Thank you. Thank you so much, Chair. And good morning, Commissioner. Good morning, Chief. Good morning, everyone. First, I also want to join in the congratulations. It's exciting to have an EMS expert at the helm. You know, we always see different expertise reflected in leadership, and this is great. My first question is around the split between FDNY EMS responses and private systems, as you mentioned. You mentioned it's about a third that's going to private systems. Sorry. I have five questions and five minutes, so we're going to try to keep the answers brief as well. So, the first question is, when are those units dispatched versus FDNY units, AND they are better paid. Do they have a different workload?

They're dispatched as part of our dispatch system so they're dispatched based on who's the closest. So, they work in particular areas. They have higher rates of pay because they work directly for the hospital. We're not paying them as City employees. They have

different packages, different benefit packages, you know, because they're private employees.

Thank you. Second question is, I'm really happy to hear the statistics regarding the declining number of fatalities. You mentioned 2022 was a high at 97, and then it went down to 62 in FY25. Could you share this information with the Committee in terms of, say, by battalion? I know I have Battalion 19 in District 14. It's about 90 percent of my District, and I'd just be very curious to see what the numbers have been there, especially, as you know, and we discussed last week, thank you for the conversation, that we've had a number of fatal fires just in the last couple of months.
Sure. We can get together and talk about the information that you need.

Thank you. And in particular, I just want to highlight as Chair of Housing and Buildings, it'd be particularly important to see when the cause of a fire is something like electrical wiring, something related to the building condition. So, as you share information with us about

fires, causes of fires across the city, very interested in seeing that. Chief Esposito, you answered Council Member Maloney's question regarding the Bronx delegation reaching out to you about a fifth firefighter. We understand that deploying three- to four-person teams takes longer than sending two five-person engines. So, in addition to, I know you said you were reviewing, but I'm curious your response to some of the ideas that we raised in the letter, if you agree or disagree with anything as stated.

You know, on the operational front, an engine staffed with five firefighters, we know will stretch an operator hose line quicker than an engine staffed with four firefighters, and we are continuing to review the proposal. It would result in a reduction of the number of engines sent on the initial call for a fire from three to two, and the theory is that that would free up some availability to respond and reduce response times for other emergencies.

Yeah, exactly. Thank you. We look forward to your response on that.

And, you know, as my colleague, no relation, Council Member Justin Sanchez said in the letter, we do, you know, want to be mindful of reducing response times and anything that can be done there. My last question, I mean, I have like three more, but I don't think I have time so I'm going to focus it on the conversation that we had last week. It feels like three years ago, but that was just a week ago, regarding the agency's coordination with additional agencies after a fire, right? I will be the first to admit, you know, I try to go to as many fires in my District. FDNY is almost always gone by the time that I get there, unless it's one of the major ones, because, you know, thankful for all of the work, you know, they put out the fire, they do their thing, and then I'm really working with my constituents to make sure people know where they're going to go for the evening, you know, what happens next, right? There's big questions. So, we've had this, you know, I want to sort of emphasize, we are having a non-legislative conversation about improvements, right? We don't have to legislate everything. But on the occasion when FDNY is responding to fires with less than three alarms, I

have noticed, and I know other Colleagues have also noticed, a gap in FDNY's, I don't know if it's the communication or the way that the agencies are working together to make sure that vacates are issued appropriately, because those vacates then trigger the more, you know, call it human side, the American Red Cross, you know, hotel for the night response. [GAVEL] So, I just am requesting an update right now on those conversations. Are any protocols going to be changing, or when can I expect a response? Thank you.

We're definitely having those conversations, and thank you for bringing that up. We're working with our partner agencies to make sure any gaps that exist will be closed. It's going to take a couple more conversations, as you can imagine. Every agency has their own protocol, and we have to see how those protocols align and where we can close some of those gaps. I think you're probably getting emails about fires now.
Yes. Thank you. So excited.
So, we've made some progress on that front, and I expect we'll continue to make progress there.

Thank you. Madam Chair, can I ask one more quick question? You talked about the criminal summons issued for a vehicle that was blocking a fire hydrant. Can you tell us where that was, first? And second, how often are trucks getting stuck behind double-parked vehicles, right, so they're not getting to their sites. Do you keep that information, and what can we do to improve that? Thank you, Madam Chair.

So, this year, we have issued several criminal court summonses for vehicles parked on hydrants. Two of them were for the fifth alarm on Finley in early January. One of those resulted in a 3,500-dollar fine. The second one is still being adjudicated. You know, we do get stuck in times behind cars and traffic, double-parked vehicles or vehicles blocking the road. Sometimes we're able to squeeze by or have to wait for the driver, and other times we have to back out of the block and go

around, and it does lead to a delay. And with the snow that we had this year and how long it stayed around, I think we all saw it, that cars were now parked further off the curb into traffic, and if there was going to be somebody double-parked or delivery trucks, it's just all of that congestion that slows us down.
Thank you, Chief. Thank you, Chair.
Council Member Maloney.

Thank you, Chair. My next question continues in the theme around replacements and maintenance. The City has a commitment to replace the engine and ladder apparatus every 10 years, and reports of supply chain disruptions and issues with manufacturing have meant there's a bit of a delay. So how many apparatuses were delivered in the last year? And then the follow-up question to that? What is the gap between what was ordered and delivered?

While Commissioner Brooks looks at that information, in the fall I was able to visit the factory that makes our fire trucks out in

Wisconsin and had a discussion with the CEO of the company. And initially, all of our apparatus had been ordered on time, and initially the delay was what everybody referred to as the global supply chain shortage. But what Seagrave had to do during the pandemic was lay off some of their workers. And as the supply chain caught up and started to deliver the parts, as they went to hire their workers back, many of them did not come back. So, the supply chain shortage has been rectified. They now have a skilled workforce issue. They would love to be working double shifts. They're just not able to at this point. They are prioritizing FDNY apparatus. We are getting consistent deliveries, and it's considerably better than it was this time last year.
And then in regards of what's being received, we're in the process of receiving eight squads, 41 pumpers, 11 tower ladders, and 22 rear mount aerials.
And what was the gap between ordered and what was actually delivered?
What do you mean, like the turnaround time? Is that what you're?
Sure.
It's about 900 days from when we submit the purchase order until we receive the vehicle.

Thank you. And my last question is around the number of women serving in FDNY continuing to grow. And many firehouses only have one locker or a single shower designated for the female firefighters and wondering if you have any comment on that regarding steps to take to make sure we have adequate facilities to accommodate more female firefighters entering.

So, like you mentioned, all our facilities have a female locker room. We are in the process of our new design specs is that we are building gender neutrality for our locations. We have already done that at a location in Brooklyn, and all our new design specs will include that. So going forward, we will have gender neutrality locker rooms for all our locations.

So, obviously, that's a big undertaking, right? We have 100-year-old buildings, and we're trying to retrofit that with new bathrooms and locker rooms so the truth of the matter is we still have space issues. Though every firehouse

has a bathroom for females, there still may be some space issues that we continue to work through. And moving forward, it's not just these firehouses and EMS system, EMS houses, stations that we have to maintain, and some of them being very old. But also moving forward, as we put new housing in, you know, we'd like to be considered for new firehouses, EMS stations, and new resources to accommodate the people in those growing areas. And that's just part of our modernizing the Fire Department and preparing our infrastructure to go for the next 50 years and handle the calls that are going to be happening all over our city.

I agree. And please understand that these issues that we're bringing up is not a knock to the Fire Department or to facilities. It is because we have a new Administration, and they need to know what's happening on the ground. And they need to know why we've asked for 1 billion dollars to be infused into the Fire Department and why we cannot afford to have any money taken out. So, how many Nederman systems are an operable ballpark, or if you know exactly.
I don't have that information in front of me.

Do you think that possibly one of your team members can get that information, maybe call over to Metro Tech? I see people putting notes on your thing. Maybe they could find that out and then find out how long you wait when you learn something is expired for an order to be put in, you know, or when you know it in advance. Because it's very important that we know that. We have to know that there is a constant chain and flow of communication when an order is called in that it is looked at immediately. So, before we get back, so does the Fire Department have a platform that tracks the priority work orders, requests, assests, and a resolution? Do you have that program or policy?
Yeah. We have a database that has all the information when a work order is called in, trades people who assess it, project managers who assess it.
Right. And are you able to get the information on the Nederman system for me?
Of course.

All right. And then right now what you've seen up here, I just have a question. If you were in these firehouses that you've seen thus far, and there are a couple more to come, would you feel safe working in that firehouse?

I'll answer that. You know, to your point, Madam Chair, the men and women that work in these houses are heroes, and they would put their life on the line and have put their life on the line for their fellow New Yorkers. They don't deserve to be in facilities like that. They don't deserve to be in the presence of mold or water infiltration. They absolutely don't. They deserve better. And we'll work with what we have to make those repairs as quickly as possible and attract those repairs. We have to move forward in a different way because these houses are getting older by the day and one repair will lead to another repair. So, we have to do a better job and I can commit to that, that we will do our part to make sure that we're on top of this, whether it be a better tracking system or, you know, certainly better communication about what our needs are for these facilities. There's a lot of facilities. So, we expect that there's going

to be these situations. But, you know, to your original question, should they be living like that? The answer is no. They should not.

Bravo. You're right. No. Okay. We're ready to go to the next slide. Okay. The next slide is Ladder 78, and they put in for an unstable front parapet wall of the firehouse numerous times. In June of 2023, the buildings unit subcontracted out a company to put a protective netting over the unstable parapet wall. No repairs have been done since the netting was put on. Previous work orders were submitted on 6/21 of '22 3/11 of '22, 12/6 of '21, and 1/25 of 2020. We're here today on March 13th of 2026, and that netting is still on. What is the cause for the delay here?

So, this particular firehouse, we had contractors out there about two weeks ago and they're in the process of coming up with a revised proposal on the cost for that. Once we receive the cost proposal, we start to work on submitting it.

All right. Do you see a pattern though? First, it takes a very long time to

get out there. Then they put up a scaffold or netting. Then they have a contractor go out. Then, what is it, six years later, contractor goes out again and because things are more expensive now, they have to do a new cost proposal for what it'll cost. Why is there such a gap from what the time that you have? Because if the money is there and you have to maintain these houses, why is there such a gap in the timeframe from when you first get a very dangerous condition reported to the time that it gets fixed? Six years is a ridiculous amount of time.
So, you have no answer? Okay, okay, no answer. Let's go to the next picture.

I just wanted to add to that to give a partial response. So, we have had our civilian headcount reduced over the years and so that certainly contributes. If you look at actual staff in facilities pre-pandemic to now, they've lost about 20 actual people, like not just vacancies, but comparing payroll headcount to payroll headcount, and that's about 18 percent of their staff, which certainly contributes to a longer time.
Is there a reason for those vacancies?

So, they were part of previous financial plan savings initiatives in order to contribute towards filling the budget gap without impacting fire and EMS, where we have taken reductions, generally speaking, has been on the civilian support staff side.
Since 2020? Since the COVID shutdown?
Yeah.
